topicName: Logic Coverage Criteria (ACC, GACC, CACC, RACC)

questions.question: In logic coverage criteria, what is the formal definition of a 'predicate'?

options.A: An expression that evaluates to a Boolean value (true or false).
options.B: A function that returns an integer.
options.C: A loop counter variable.
options.D: A string concatenation operator.

questions.explanation: A predicate is an expression that evaluates to a Boolean value. It may contain Boolean variables, relational operators (<, >, ==), and logical connectives (AND, OR, NOT).

questions.question: What is a 'clause' in a Boolean predicate?

options.A: A sub-expression that does not contain any logical operators (AND, OR, NOT).
options.B: Any expression that contains an if-statement.
options.C: A complete Java class.
options.D: A loop condition.

questions.explanation: A clause is an atomic Boolean expression that contains no logical operators. E.g., in ((x > 0) || y), '(x > 0)' and 'y' are individual clauses.

questions.question: What does Predicate Coverage (PC) require?

options.A: For each predicate p, TR contains two requirements: p evaluates to true, and p evaluates to false.
options.B: Every clause in the predicate must be true.
options.C: Every clause must be evaluated 2^N times.
options.D: Predicates must only contain AND operators.

questions.explanation: Predicate Coverage (PC) requires test cases that make the entire predicate evaluate to true at least once, and to false at least once.

questions.question: What does Clause Coverage (CC) require?

options.A: For each individual clause c in predicate p, TR contains two requirements: c evaluates to true, and c evaluates to false.
options.B: The whole predicate must evaluate to true.
options.C: Only the first clause in the predicate is tested.
options.D: All clauses must be true at the same time.

questions.explanation: Clause Coverage (CC) requires that each individual clause in the predicate evaluates to true at least once and false at least once.

questions.question: Does Clause Coverage (CC) subsume Predicate Coverage (PC)?

options.A: No! CC does not subsume PC, and PC does not subsume CC.
options.B: Yes, CC always subsumes PC.
options.C: Yes, PC always subsumes CC.
options.D: Only when the predicate has 1 clause.

questions.explanation: Surprisingly, CC does not subsume PC! E.g. in p = a OR b, tests {(a=T, b=F), (a=F, b=T)} satisfy CC, but p evaluates to true in both tests! Thus PC is not satisfied.

questions.question: How many test cases are required to satisfy Combinatorial Coverage (CoC) for a predicate with N independent clauses?

options.D: N!

questions.explanation: Combinatorial Coverage (CoC) requires testing every possible combination of truth assignments to the N clauses, which equals 2^N tests.

questions.question: When is a clause c said to 'determine' predicate p?

options.A: When toggling the truth value of c changes the truth value of p (with all minor clauses held fixed).
options.B: When c is the longest clause.
options.C: When c evaluates to true.
options.D: When c is an arithmetic expression.

questions.explanation: Clause c determines p if and only if: changing the truth value of c while keeping the values of all other clauses fixed causes the evaluation of p to invert.

questions.question: In Active Clause Coverage (ACC), what are 'major clauses' and 'minor clauses'?

options.A: For each requirement, one clause is chosen as the 'major clause' (the clause being tested for determination), while the remaining clauses are 'minor clauses'.
options.B: Major clauses are in main(); minor clauses are in subroutines.
options.C: Major clauses contain relational operators; minor clauses contain variables.
options.D: Major clauses evaluate to true; minor clauses evaluate to false.

questions.explanation: When testing a specific clause c under ACC, c is designated as the major clause. All other clauses in that predicate are minor clauses.

questions.question: What is General Active Clause Coverage (GACC)?

options.A: For each major clause c, choose minor clauses such that c determines p. The minor clauses do NOT have to take the same truth values when c is true as when c is false.
options.B: Minor clauses must be identical in both tests.
options.C: All clauses must be active simultaneously.
options.D: Predicate must evaluate to false in both tests.

questions.explanation: In GACC, clause c must determine p when c=T and when c=F, but the values assigned to minor clauses in the c=T test are allowed to differ from the c=F test.

questions.question: What is the defining condition of Restricted Active Clause Coverage (RACC)?

options.A: The values assigned to the minor clauses MUST be strictly identical in the test where c is true and in the test where c is false.
options.B: The predicate must contain at most 2 clauses.
options.C: The predicate cannot contain the NOT operator.
options.D: The test suite must be restricted to 1 test case.

questions.explanation: RACC restricts minor clauses to remain exactly identical in both the c=true and c=false tests for major clause c.

questions.question: What is Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC)?

options.A: For each major clause c, minor clauses are chosen such that p evaluates to true when c is true (or false), and p evaluates to false when c is false (or true), but minor clauses may differ between the two tests.
options.B: All clauses must be mathematically correlated.
options.C: CACC is identical to Predicate Coverage.
options.D: CACC requires 2^N tests.

questions.explanation: CACC requires that toggling major clause c in the test pair causes predicate p to toggle as well, while allowing minor clauses to differ between the two tests.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly orders the Active Clause Coverage criteria by strength?

options.A: RACC subsumes CACC, CACC subsumes GACC.
options.B: GACC subsumes CACC, CACC subsumes RACC.
options.C: CACC subsumes RACC, RACC subsumes GACC.
options.D: GACC subsumes PC, but RACC does not.

questions.explanation: RACC imposes the strictest requirement (identical minor clauses). Any test pair satisfying RACC satisfies CACC. CACC guarantees the predicate toggles, satisfying GACC.

questions.question: Does GACC guarantee Predicate Coverage (PC)?

options.A: No! In GACC, it is possible for p to evaluate to true (or false) in both the c=T and c=F tests if minor clauses change between tests.
options.B: Yes, GACC always guarantees PC.
options.C: Only if N = 2.
options.D: Only when the predicate has no AND operators.

questions.explanation: Under GACC, minor clauses may differ between the two tests, which can result in the predicate evaluating to True in both tests. Thus GACC does NOT subsume PC!

questions.question: Do CACC and RACC guarantee Predicate Coverage (PC)?

options.A: Yes, both CACC and RACC guarantee that p evaluates to True in one test and False in the other.
options.B: No, neither does.
options.C: Only RACC does.
options.D: Only CACC does.

questions.explanation: Both CACC and RACC explicitly require that the predicate evaluates to opposite truth values in the test pair, directly satisfying Predicate Coverage.

questions.question: For predicate p = A ∧ B, what truth assignment to minor clause B makes major clause A determine p?

options.A: B must be TRUE.
options.B: B must be FALSE.
options.C: B can be either TRUE or FALSE.
options.D: B must be null.

questions.explanation: If B is FALSE, p = A ∧ F = F regardless of A (A has no effect). If B is TRUE, p = A ∧ T = A. Thus, A determines p if and only if B is TRUE.

questions.question: For predicate p = A ∨ B, what truth assignment to minor clause B makes major clause A determine p?

options.A: B must be FALSE.
options.B: B must be TRUE.
options.C: B can be either TRUE or FALSE.
options.D: B must be undefined.

questions.explanation: If B is TRUE, p = A ∨ T = T regardless of A. If B is FALSE, p = A ∨ F = A. Thus, A determines p if and only if B is FALSE.

questions.question: What is Inactive Clause Coverage (ICC)?

options.A: Tests where minor clauses are chosen such that major clause c does NOT determine the predicate p.
options.B: Tests where no code is executed.
options.C: Testing dead code.
options.D: Testing inactive user sessions.

questions.explanation: Inactive Clause Coverage tests situations where the major clause is prevented from determining the predicate by the configuration of minor clauses.

questions.question: Why is Combinatorial Coverage (CoC) impractical for predicates with many clauses (e.g. N = 10)?

options.A: Because 2^10 = 1024 tests are required for a single decision predicate, leading to combinatorial explosion.
options.B: Because compilers limit predicates to 5 clauses.
options.C: Because CoC does not test all clauses.
options.D: Because CoC cannot be used with boolean variables.

questions.explanation: 2^N grows exponentially. For N=10, 1024 test cases are needed for just one condition. Active Clause Coverage criteria provide rigorous testing with approximately 2N tests.

questions.question: What is the Minimum Number of tests required for RACC on a predicate with N independent clauses?

options.A: N + 1 tests (by sharing tests among different major clauses).
options.B: 2^N tests.
options.C: 1 test.
options.D: N! tests.

questions.explanation: Each major clause requires 2 tests (one T, one F). By carefully sharing test cases between different major clauses, RACC can often be satisfied with as few as N + 1 tests.

questions.question: Which of the following Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) software safety standards requires Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC), which is closely related to RACC/CACC?

options.A: DO-178B / DO-178C (Level A avionics software)
options.B: ISO 9001
options.C: IEEE 802.11
options.D: PCI-DSS

questions.explanation: DO-178B/C Level A avionics safety mandates MC/DC (which corresponds directly to Correlated / Restricted Active Clause Coverage) for flight-critical code.
